items.question: What is LINQ, and how do query syntax and method syntax relate?
items.answer: LINQ queries any IEnumerable or IQueryable source with compile-time types. Query expressions compile to the same extension methods as method chains — identical IL and iterator allocations. Operators without keywords (Count, TryGetNonEnumeratedCount, ToList) stay as methods. Neither spelling talks to SQL unless the source is IQueryable from a provider.
followUps: Which style do you prefer for joins?
items.sixtySeconds: Same operators, same cost. Query is sugar. Methods for Count and operators without keywords.

items.question: Explain deferred execution and a hot-path bug you have seen.
items.answer: A query variable stores a plan. Each enumeration re-runs the chain and allocates iterators (WhereIterator, Func delegates). Count then foreach on the same IEnumerable is two passes — on a live submit buffer, results differ between passes. ToList once to snapshot. TryGetNonEnumeratedCount avoids a full walk for Count on List/array when you also need to iterate.
followUps: What allocates in a three-operator chain?
items.sixtySeconds: Plan versus run. Each foreach re-runs and allocates. ToList to freeze. Count then foreach is two passes.

items.question: What is TryGetNonEnumeratedCount and when does it help?
items.answer: Extension method that returns true when the underlying source already knows Count — List<T>, arrays, ICollection — without enumerating a deferred chain. Returns false for pure Where/Select pipelines; then materialize with ToList if you need both count and iteration. Avoids double enumeration on hot reporting paths.
followUps: What happens when it returns false?
Is it the same as ICollection.Count?
items.sixtySeconds: True when source knows count without walking deferred chain. False on pure LINQ plan — then ToList once.

items.question: IEnumerable versus IQueryable — what actually differs?
items.answer: IEnumerable operators take Func delegates and run LINQ to Objects in-process with iterator allocations. IQueryable operators take Expression<Func<...>> trees; a provider may translate to SQL or throw. AsQueryable on List<T> still runs locally. ToList/AsEnumerable is the materialization wall — after it, full C# Func LINQ runs on pulled data.
followUps: Why do local functions fail in IQueryable Where?
items.sixtySeconds: Func in memory versus Expression for provider. ToList is the wall. AsQueryable on List is still local.

items.question: What does SelectMany buy you that Select does not?
items.answer: Select maps one-to-one. SelectMany maps one-to-many and flattens — two from clauses in query syntax. Select of a collection yields IEnumerable<TInner> nested; SelectMany yields flat TInner. GroupBy after SelectMany buffers the entire flattened sequence before first yield.
followUps: How do you keep the outer element while flattening?
items.sixtySeconds: SelectMany flattens. Two from clauses. Length is sum of inners, not outer count.

items.question: Which operators stream versus buffer?
items.answer: Where, Select, SelectMany, Take stream as they read — still one iterator object per operator. OrderBy, GroupBy, Reverse buffer the entire source before first yield. Knowing the difference prevents assuming GroupBy is cheap streaming on large attempt lists.
followUps: Does OrderBy allocate the full sorted buffer?
items.sixtySeconds: Where/Select stream. OrderBy/GroupBy buffer all first. Plan hot paths accordingly.

items.question: When is LINQ to Objects the right choice versus IQueryable?
items.answer: CSV import, Redis JSON, File.ReadLines after ToList, and any data already in memory — full C# in Func lambdas. IQueryable is for translatable predicates on remote stores. Copy-pasting in-memory LINQ to IQueryable fails at runtime with NotSupportedException. Materialize with ToList, then enrich with StringComparison and custom methods.
items.sixtySeconds: In-memory data = LINQ to Objects. Remote = translatable IQueryable. ToList wall before rich C#.

items.question: What iterator allocations should you worry about on a submit path?
items.answer: Each deferred operator wraps the previous in a new iterator and captures lambdas as delegates — three operators means three iterator layers plus delegate allocations. Struct enumerators box when API returns IEnumerable<T>. Fixes: fold filters into one Where, ToList once at boundary, TryGetNonEnumeratedCount for count, or for-loop/Span after measurement. dotMemory shows WhereIterator and Func allocations.
followUps: Is LINQ always slower than foreach?
When do you escape to Span?
items.sixtySeconds: Each operator adds iterator + delegate. Snapshot once. Measure with dotMemory before micro-optimizing.

items.question: When would you mention PLINQ (AsParallel)?
items.answer: Only as a measured opt-in for CPU-bound aggregation on a large in-memory snapshot — after ToList, when profiling shows single-threaded LINQ is the bottleneck. AsParallel partitions locally; ordering is nondeterministic unless AsOrdered. Not for IQueryable, not for small collections, not the first answer to deferred execution bugs. Pointer only in this module.
items.sixtySeconds: PLINQ is measured CPU-bound opt-in on in-memory snapshots. Not default. Not for IQueryable.
